analysis.one_liner: Narrows the definition of a 'joint employer,' shielding franchisors and staffing firms from responsibility for workers' pay and conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate committee it was referred to.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal labor law, a company can sometimes be treated as a 'joint employer' of workers it doesn't directly hire — for example, a fast-food corporation that sets menu prices, technology, and brand standards for its franchisees' workers. This bill would rewrite the law so a company counts as a joint employer only if it directly controls hiring, firing, pay, supervision, scheduling, or discipline. That would mean workers at a McDonald's franchise could no longer bargain with, or sue, the corporation itself — only the local franchise owner. The same rule would apply to temp and staffing arrangements under wage-and-hour law.
analysis.who_benefits: Large franchisors, staffing agencies, contractors, and subcontractors gain: they keep setting the business terms that shape workers' jobs while shedding legal responsibility for wages, working conditions, and union bargaining. Franchise chains gain a shield from lawsuits and labor disputes involving franchisee employees.

how_it_helps.text: Under the bill, a company is a joint employer only if it 'directly, actually, and immediately' exercises significant control over hiring, firing, pay, benefits, day-to-day supervision, scheduling, or discipline [S2][S3].
This narrower test would apply to both the National Labor Relations Act, which governs union organizing and bargaining, and the Fair Labor Standards Act, which governs minimum wage and overtime [S3].

For a franchisor, the effect is to make the local franchise owner the sole legal employer, so a worker's wage claim or union dispute stays with a small business rather than the national brand [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers in franchised chains, temp and staffing arrangements, and subcontracted jobs lose a legal route to hold the big company at the top accountable when wages go unpaid or conditions worsen; unions lose the ability to bargain with the corporation that actually sets the economics. Workers would bear any unpaid wages or lost bargaining power that the smaller employer cannot cover.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes joint liability, meaning a franchisee or staffing firm that cannot pay a judgment leaves workers with no recovery from the corporation that shaped their job [S3].

Supporters' case: the existing broader standard can make a franchisor legally liable for employment decisions it did not actually make, which they argue discourages franchising and burdens small franchise owners [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill is written broadly: 'direct, actual, and immediate' control over essential terms would exclude routine indirect control — like a chain's brand-wide wage floors or scheduling software — that currently supports joint-employer findings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is legal clarity and reduced liability for franchisors and staffing firms. The cost falls on workers, who would lose one of the few ways to reach the well-capitalized company that actually sets their job's economics. The bill's remedies are one-directional: it narrows employer responsibility without adding any new worker protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law and never even received a hearing, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, with 14 Republican cosponsors including Sens. Braun, Cassidy, Rubio, and Scott of Florida [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers in franchised, temporary, and subcontracted jobs keep the broader joint-employer legal route; franchisors and staffing firms gained nothing they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, since the bill never advanced

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: Franchise and small-business lobbying groups
for.role: Industry advocates for a narrower joint-employer test
for.what_they_did: Backed versions of this bill in Congress as part of a long-running campaign to reverse broader joint-employer standards.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or independent supported it, and the bill never advanced beyond referral.

industries.industry: Franchise corporations (fast food, hotels, retail chains)
industries.note: The bill would let franchisors keep setting brand standards and economics while the local franchise owner alone is the legal employer, ending worker claims and union bargaining directed at the corporation. Workers lose a route to the company with the deepest pockets.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing and labor subcontracting firms
industries.note: A narrower joint-employer test under the Fair Labor Standards Act would limit client companies' wage-and-hour liability for temp and contract workers, reducing pressure on staffing arrangements to pay lawful wages.

Under the National Labor Relations Act, unions currently can bargain with a corporation that meaningfully controls franchisee or subcontractor workplaces; the bill would confine bargaining to the immediate employer.
